question:
A circle of radius \(5\) is inscribed in a rectangle as shown. The ratio of the length of the rectangle to its width is \(2:1.\) What is the area of the rectangle?

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_12B_Q02_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Interpret “inscribed” in the sense illustrated: the circle is tangent to the rectangle's two long sides.

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_12B_Q02_question_fig1.svg)

The distance between those sides is the circle's diameter, so the rectangle's width is \(2\cdot5=10\). The length-to-width ratio is \(2:1\), so its length is \(2\cdot10=20\). Its area is therefore
\[
20\cdot10=\boxed{200}.
\]
Strictly, an inscribed circle touches all four sides. That would make both rectangle dimensions equal to the diameter \(10\), contradicting the given \(2:1\) ratio. Thus the illustrated interpretation gives \(\boxed{200}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\); the strict interpretation has no such rectangle.

The target explicitly distinguishes boundary length from area. Perimeter meaning is required for that contrast, not all rectangle/square perimeter computations.
Two-digit columns support larger numerical areas. Repeated unit-square counts or decomposed multiplication can also compute an area, so no fixed dimension range is imposed by this preparation link.

edges.reason: The rectangle/square area formulas count equal square units, so the meaning of area and its uniform unit are part of the asserted result.

edges.reason: Fraction division prepares ratio values with fractional terms. The target expressly permits a simple ratio, and a whole-number pair such as 6 to 3 needs only ordinary division; no fraction-by-fraction division is universal.
